questions.q: What does Ledger prove that SQL Auditing (Lesson 36) cannot, by itself?
options: Ledger and SQL Auditing do exactly the same thing
Which rows changed since a given point in time
That a table's history hasn't been tampered with, cryptographically — auditing only records what happened, without proving the record itself is genuine
Ledger removes the need for any data encryption
questions.explain: An audit log could theoretically be altered by someone with enough access; Ledger's cryptographic digest lets you verify the history is genuine, even against sysadmin.

questions.q: Why is Change Tracking NOT a security or compliance feature, despite tracking which rows changed?
options: Change Tracking is actually identical to Ledger
It's lightweight by design — no full history of values, no cryptographic proof — built purely for synchronization scenarios, not compliance
Change Tracking requires the same setup as SQL Auditing
Change Tracking cannot track any changes at all
questions.explain: Change Tracking answers "which rows changed since I last checked" for sync purposes — it makes no integrity or audit-trail claims.

questions.q: In the healthcare compliance scenario, why does no single Chapter 6 tool satisfy the entire requirement alone?
options: The scenario can be solved with Change Tracking alone
Each tool (TDE, classification, masking, auditing, Ledger) answers a different specific piece of the compliance question — none substitutes for the others
Only TDE is actually needed; the other tools are redundant
Compliance scenarios never require more than one security feature
questions.explain: Encryption-at-rest, classification, masking, logging, and tamper-evidence are five genuinely different protections, each covering a different part of the requirement.

questions.q: Why would Change Tracking fail to satisfy an auditor asking for proof that a table's history wasn't tampered with?
options: It only tracks which rows changed for sync purposes — it keeps no cryptographic proof and makes no tamper-evidence claim at all
Change Tracking already provides the exact same cryptographic proof Ledger does
Change Tracking is disabled by default and can never be enabled
Auditors never ask about tamper-evidence
questions.explain: Change Tracking and Ledger solve genuinely different problems — reaching for the wrong one is a real, common mistake this lesson calls out directly.
